**Text**  
Matching the Topic. The passage describes a trip to an unusual mountain village, the travelers’ feelings, and an encounter with an old woman – exactly the kind of narrative the prompt “a story about an unusual holiday trip” calls for. 4/5  
Logic & Commonsense. The story is mostly coherent, but there is a minor inconsistency: Mark is described as “lazy and just wanted to relax” yet later “was worried about the cold weather,” which mixes laziness with a specific concern and feels slightly odd. Only one such logical slip is present. 4/5  
Vocabulary & Grammar. The text is fluent; only a tiny awkwardness (“the village was surprisingly attractive”) but no grammatical errors. 5/5  

---  
**Q1**  
Logic & Commonsense. The question asks why the traveler was nervous; the answer options are plausible and fit the scenario. No commonsense conflict. 5/5  
Vocabulary & Grammar. The question and all options are well‑formed, no errors. 5/5  
Text-Based Answerability. The correct answer (unfamiliar village/language) is directly stated (“I was scared at first because the locals spoke a different language”). 5/5  
Reading Dependency. Without the text a test‑taker could guess “different language” but would have no certainty; the text is needed to choose confidently. 4/5  
Answer Unambiguity. Only one option matches the text; the others are clearly unrelated. 5/5  
Distractor Plausibility. Distractor 1 (“weather was very cold”) is plausible because Mark worries about cold, but the traveler does not; distractor 2 and 3 are less plausible. Overall, two are plausible, one less so. 4/5  
Using Paraphrases. The correct answer rephrases the passage (“different language” → “locals spoke a different language”) with more than two word changes. 5/5  
Explanation Quality. The explanation states why the correct answer matches the text and why each distractor is unsupported; it covers all three distractors. 5/5  

---  
**Q2**  
Logic & Commonsense. The question is sensible; the options are realistic actions an old woman could take. 5/5  
Vocabulary & Grammar. No errors in wording of question or options. 5/5  
Text-Based Answerability. The text says she “showed us how to make creative lanterns from local flowers,” which directly supports the correct answer. 5/5  
Reading Dependency. A guesser might think an old woman would give directions or a meal, but the specific “make lanterns from flowers” is unlikely without reading. 4/5  
Answer Unambiguity. Only one option matches the text; the others describe different activities. 5/5  
Distractor Plausibility. All three distractors are plausible actions for a helpful villager, making them believable to someone who skimmed. 5/5  
Using Paraphrases. The correct answer paraphrases “make creative lanterns from local flowers” as “create decorative items using flowers,” changing several words while keeping meaning. 5/5  
Explanation Quality. The explanation correctly links the correct answer to the text and explains why each distractor is unsupported. 5/5  

---  
**Q3**  
Logic & Commonsense. The question is logical; the options represent different possible interests. 5/5  
Vocabulary & Grammar. Wording is clear and error‑free. 5/5  
Text-Based Answerability. The passage states “Mark… was lazy and just wanted to relax,” directly supporting the correct answer. 5/5  
Reading Dependency. Without the text a test‑taker could guess Mark might prefer rest, but the specific “lazy” detail is only in the passage, so guessing is harder. 4/5  
Answer Unambiguity. Only one option reflects the text; the others introduce unsupported ideas. 5/5  
Distractor Plausibility. Distractor 1 (photography) and 3 (missed modern comforts) are plausible personal interests, while distractor 2 (fear of heights) is less plausible; overall, most are believable. 4/5  
Using Paraphrases. The correct answer restates “lazy… wanted to relax” as “He wanted to rest because he was lazy,” a solid paraphrase with several word changes. 5/5  
Explanation Quality. The explanation identifies why the correct answer matches the text and why each distractor lacks textual support. 5/5  

---  
**Text Coverage**  
The three questions each target a different segment: Q1 focuses on the traveler’s initial nerves, Q2 on the old woman’s assistance, and Q3 on Mark’s attitude. All major ideas are sampled, with no part overly dominant. 5/5
